rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all 10 compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to test selectivity in the crowded central cluster. The current elution window leaves ample time margin, so resolving the two deficient pairs is the priority.

Test a further 5 C increase to improve the remaining critical pair while checking whether the preceding central pair loses too much resolution. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate temperature-dependent selectivity.

Make the gradient shallower at 55 C to improve the newly limiting central pair while preserving the pair that just reached R = 1.54. The last peak currently elutes at 6.58 min, leaving room to gain resolution without a time penalty.
Test the intermediate gradient duration: the 10- and 14-minute results suggest it may bring both critical pairs above R = 1.5. It should also keep the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is already reached; now test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten elution while retaining full resolution. Keep temperature and gradient duration fixed to measure the effect on the two marginal central pairs.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to recover the resolution lost at the higher starting organic fraction. This tests whether full resolution can be restored with an elution time competitive with injection 5, which remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Keep injection 5 as the maximum-score benchmark and explore a faster, hotter gradient. This tests whether temperature-driven elution-order changes can separate the central cluster on the opposite side of its selectivity crossover.
Explore lower-temperature selectivity with a shorter gradient to seek a faster fully resolved method on a different elution-order branch. Injection 5 remains the established maximum-score method.

Test moderately cooler conditions with a shallower gradient to separate the central cluster without the extensive crowding seen at 25 C. This explores an alternative selectivity region while retaining injection 5 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Test whether a substantially higher starting organic fraction changes central-cluster selectivity enough to obtain full resolution with faster elution. Returning to 40 C explores the opposite side of the temperature-driven crossover, while injection 5 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Test a higher starting organic fraction at 60 C to shift the crowded central peaks away from their selectivity crossover while keeping elution fast. Injection 5 remains the fully resolved, maximum-score fallback.

Increase starting organic by one step to try to separate the remaining critical central pair in the fast 60 C method. Monitor the first pair closely, since its resolution may decrease as early retention is reduced.

Return to the near-resolved conditions of injection 7 and reduce the endpoint by one grid step to recover its R = 1.47 pair. This should test a second maximum-score method with more balanced resolution margins while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test a steeper gradient at 35 C to move the nearly coeluting central pair away from the crossover seen in injection 10. This explores a potentially faster selectivity branch while preserving injections 5 and 14 as maximum-score methods.

Narrow the gradient window and shorten its programmed duration while preserving injection 5's slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute. Since all peaks previously eluted before this new gradient ends at the outlet, full resolution and the maximum CRF should be retained.

Preserve the proven gradient slope through the crowded peaks, then hold at 50% organic to test a shorter programmed gradient and lower solvent endpoint. The final compound may elute later, but the established 7.60-minute result leaves some margin before the time penalty begins.

Increase the slope slightly from the fully resolved injection 16 to test the nearest faster gradient at this duration. This probes the resolution boundary more finely than the previously unsuccessful 10-minute gradient ending at 95% organic.

Back off to the proven slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute while shortening the programmed gradient to eight minutes. Unlike the six-minute version, this gradient should continue through the last peak and retain both full resolution and the 7.60-minute elution time.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step from the fully resolved injection 14 to seek shorter elution while retaining its improved critical-pair margin. Check both the central cluster and the first pair for loss of resolution.

Test a slope between injections 7 and 14 to seek full resolution with a shorter elution time than injection 14. The central-pair trends suggest this setting could balance both critical resolutions just above 1.5.

Raise temperature one step from the fully resolved injection 21 to test whether its narrower gradient window permits faster elution without losing resolution. Retain injection 5 as the fastest established maximum-score method if the central pair deteriorates.

Return to 55 C and slightly flatten injection 14's gradient to test a larger resolution margin for its earlier critical pair while monitoring the later pair. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, preserving maximum CRF if both pairs stay resolved.

Flatten injection 20's gradient to recover its limiting central pair while exploiting the other critical pair's larger resolution margin. This tests a potentially more robust maximum-score alternative; injection 5 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.

Lower the endpoint one step from injection 24 to bring its R = 1.41 pair above 1.5 while retaining the other critical pair's margin. The last peak is expected before 10 minutes, offering another maximum-score method; injection 5 remains the fastest proven fully resolved option.
